#3460. Every Playable Video Game in GTA 6, Ranked Worst to Best

Why rob a bank when you can play Time Jackers?

Grand Theft Auto 6 is so big that it’s actually five games in one. Like previous games in the series, there are several games-within-the-game that you can play while hanging out in Leonida. These aren’t just quick arcade games that you can play for a few minutes, but full-on console games that are actually pretty fun in their own right.

It’s a playful meta joke from Rockstar, and I would be remiss not to play into it. Where there are games, there must be a video game website ranking those games in an arbitrary list. Here’s how the four games featured in GTA 6 stack up. Even if they aren’t all winners, they’re all at least high-effort jokes that deserve some praise.

As a parody of the kind of hunting games you find in dive bars, Bang For Your Buck is a pretty one-note gag. It’s an on-rails shooter where you simply have to gun down bucks while sparing does that populate three stages. The only real twist is that your money ticks down along with the timer, so you need to kill deer rapidly to keep playing. That mechanic is reused for a much better game that you’ll see higher on this list, so Bang For Your Buck doesn’t have much going for it beyond the obvious hunting satire. But as a piece of worldbuilding? It’s pure Florida, and I’m glad that it exists in Leonida.

Street Trash 3: Dezombifier is GTA 6’s very own Vampire Survivors clone. It’s a top-down twin-stick shooter where the goal is to gun through dense waves of zombies (and skeletons, for some reason) as you hunt for gears. As a send-up, it’s a little hit-and-miss. The roguelite is fun enough with its reliable choose-three level-up system, though it could have benefited from adopting Vampire Survivors’ more intuitive auto-firing action. It’s a little less effective as satire than some other entries on his list, since it feels more like a parody of AAA action games, complete with its quippy narrator. Still, it’s a fun little distraction that even has its own unlock system to keep you playing and find new weapons.

Arguably the funniest and most unexpected gag in all of GTA 6, Tenebrae Lux is Rockstar at the height of its satirical powers. The black-and-white puzzle game is a send-up of arthouse indie games created by auteur developers. More specifically, it’s a parody of Jonathan Blow, the creator of The Witness and Order of the Sinking Star. The convoluted experience (created solely by fictional developer Johannes Zuch) sees you exploring a mysterious island as a pompous narrator waxes poetic about philosophy. Funny enough, it’s a pretty well-designed puzzle game with galaxy-brained solutions. While it’s debatably a little too cerebral to enjoy casually, it’s an undeniably great spoof that respects this kind of game enough to lampoon them so perfectly.

The better of GTA 6’s two twin-stick shooters, Time Jackers Rewind is an over-the-top sci-fi game. A wisecracking soldier’s attempt to take down DominiCorp hits a snag when he accidentally travels through time. He gets some time powers in the process, but the twist is that he will die if he runs out of juice. You can only top it off by killing mutants, which basically makes Time Jackers Rewind a Crank video game in my book. It's a fast-paced shooter that pushes you to perfect your route through the city as you strategically acquire enough power to stay alive. It’s just a great mechanical premise, even if you take away the loudmouthed hero who is constantly tossing out hilariously hammy one-liners.

#3459. Arnold Schwarzenegger's Son Joseph Baena Joins 'Baywatch' in Surprise Role

Joseph Baena is joining Fox’s Baywatch revival in a surprise role.

“I’m Livvy Dunne’s boyfriend in the show,” Baena, 29, exclusively told Us on the set of Celebrity Weakest Link. “And she was amazing — such a great talent and she was such a talented and special gymnast. To see her in Baywatch was great.”

Baena continued to gush over his onscreen love interest and other costars.

“She killed it. As did the rest of the cast,” he added. “Thaddeus [LaGrone], Noah Beck and everyone else is doing a phenomenal job. It was amazing to spend time with them on set and work out with them on set. I’m just really excited for the episode to come out of the whole show.”

While Arnold Schwarzenegger‘s son had a small role as Pete in season 1, he hinted he would love to see “a little more” of the character in a potential second season, adding, “We have to make the plot line [happen]. I get that — in the first season — they need to establish everyone. Maybe in the second season they can have a little fun and bring Pete back.”

The original Baywatch ran from 1989 to 2001 and showcased the lives of lifeguards who dealt with unusual circumstances — from shark attacks to serial killers — on beaches in California and Hawaii.

“I was too young to watch it live when it came out [on] TV, but I have such a connection to David Hasselhoff when he was in the SpongeBob movie. It’s one of my favorite movies of all time and such a big part of my childhood,” Baena recalled. “Especially when David Hasselhoff comes out in the show and is the speedboat to take SpongeBob back to Bikini Bottom. It’s awesome.”

He continued: “So the fact that they brought the show back and are reviving it, it was such a cool announcement. I got so excited. I wanted to audition. I unfortunately didn’t even get a chance to audition until they had already started the show. I’m so grateful that I was able to make an appearance in one of the episodes.”

The guest appearance made Baena want to do more scripted projects. For now, TV viewers can catch Baena on the Monday, November 23, episode of Fox’s Celebrity Weakness Link.

“Non-scripted reality TV has been super fun. I think I have a good personality for it,” he told Us. “Celeb Weakest Link is [an] amazing show. And I did Dancing With the Stars — that was phenomenal. It was such an amazing time.”

Baena noted that the “main vision” for his career is to be a leading man.

“To be in scripted movies, film and TV. I’ve been doing theater for a little while. I’ve been doing acting classes for a long time and just working my way up,” said the actor, who has also been working on a cookbook inspired by what he learned from mom Mildred Baena. “I’m paying my dues and I know how it goes in the industry. It’s difficult, and you never know when your time is, but I think my time is coming soon.”

He concluded: “We have some great projects coming up. Baywatch, a great horror film coming out hopefully next year. We’ll see what happens. But these are the main goals and I am ready to work for it.”

Celebrity Weakest Link airs on Fox Mondays at 9 p.m. ET.

Could the original trio get back together?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rupert Grint is the latest cast member from the Harry Potter films to join the Broadway run of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, right on the heels of Tom Felton's successful run. With Ron Weasley in tow, he's already fielding questions about whether Emma Watson and Danielle Radcliffe could be next to join the stage play.

The actor, who will reprise his role as Ron for the production, confirmed it would be his last time playing the character. As such, Collider wanted to know if there was a chance of his former famous co-stars joining. Grint didn't say definitively one way or another, but offered up this:

It would be fun. I don't know. I mean, it's obviously different for everyone. It was an intense time. When we finished, I really enjoyed stepping away and not really even thinking about it, because it was such an intense… I mean, it was enjoyable, and they looked after us, but it was a big part of us. So, yeah, maybe. I don't know. It'd be fun.

I'm sure the last thing Grint wanted to do was try to put the pressure on Radcliffe and Watson to say no, knowing the complicated thoughts both may have about returning. Daniel Radcliffe has been pretty adamant about refusing any opportunities to return, and Emma Watson has shied away from acting so much that there were rumors a few years back that she had retired.

People are always free to change their minds of course, and Rupert Grint is evidence of that. He initially said he'd only return if everyone else did, and now he's in a position where he's being asked whether his co-stars will join him onstage for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He talked about his return and how he felt immediately after the film franchise ended way back when:

Yeah. It's funny. It's interesting, going back. I spent so much time after finishing Potter kind of moving away from it and doing other things, which I've really enjoyed doing, but I think now it's a very different role in a very different context. And weirdly, it's kind of lined up that I'm the exact age of the character in that story, so it's just felt like a good time.

It does feel like a good time, what with a new Harry Potter TV show on the way. The series' arrival on the 2026 TV schedule will likely spark even more interest than usual in the franchise, and possibly encourage a lot of millennials craving nostalgia to see Grint back as Ron.

Timing aside, I'm sure it doesn't surprise anyone that actors love to work. For Rupert Grint, the return to being on stage pulls back to his start as a child actor, and that's going to be a great joy for him:

And I love New York and being on stage. It's been a while since I've done that, and it's a very important thing to me. It was my childhood, and I have a very strong connection to that character and that world. I think I'm not going to get many other opportunities to play him again. It probably is my last, and I think it'll be fun.

It should be fun, especially given what Ron Weasley is up to in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He's running the joke shop Fred and George founded, while his wife Hermione is the literal Minister of Magic. As far as acting is concerned, it's more of a supportive role, but one that Rupert Grint will likely bring a special sparkle to.

I'm still waiting to see if Grint, Emma Watson, or Daniel Radcliffe will show up in the Potter TV series. Part of me thinks they'd do it for the fans, but at the same time, I could see them wanting the new cast to have a chance to do their own thing, without drawing attention to themselves. I guess all we can do is wait and see what happens!

Rupert Grint's run on Broadway in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child kicks off on February 2nd and will end on May 30th. I'm sure getting a ticket could be a struggle, but I'm eager to see what the demand will be for fans to see one of the core stars back in the franchise!

#3457. Bringing Austen, Wharton, and Steinbeck Into the iPhone Age

It’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.

“You know [how] you look at some faces, like Rosamund Pike’s face—it looks like it’s never seen an iPhone? It looks like it’s seen a lute and a loom,” Alderton tells Frost.

“So actors who look like they’re comfortable in a period show, rather than feeling inherently modern,” says Frost, as understanding dawns. Alderton and Kazan affirm her: “Yes, yes. Exactly.”

Now that Frost gets it, she turns back to the group’s Zoom screen. “Sorry, what was the question?”

Kazan began her career as an actor, while Alderton started out as a dating columnist and Frost was a sculptor and painter. Now all three are overseeing vastly different but comparable Netflix period dramas, each based on a classic work of literature: East of Eden (Kazan’s, which was released October 1), Pride and Prejudice (Alderton’s, out December 3), and The Age of Innocence (Frost’s, coming February 18). They’ve gathered in a London conference room at Netflix headquarters for a roundtable discussion about art, work, the unique experience of adapting a beloved book—and, apparently, iPhone face.

Though this is the first time the trio has met face to face, their conversation flows so easily and naturally that interrupting them with questions sometimes feels impolite. Early on, I note that all three of these novels are, on some level, about unconventional women. Alderton, Frost, and Kazan pause for a moment, considering this Lit 101–level observation.

And then they’re off to more interesting topics.

Vanity Fair: Have you read each other’s books?

Dolly Alderton: No, I haven’t read either of your books.

Alderton: Did you read them at school, or did you read them for fun?

Frost: Pride and Prejudice I read when I was a teenager at school. East of Eden I read first about 15 years ago, I think.

Alderton: So Em already wins the round table.

Frost: And for both of you, was it the thing you most wanted to adapt?

Alderton: I would never have dared to dream to. I was so overwhelmed when I was first approached. I just thought, it’s such a precious IP. It would be way too much, and I wouldn’t be the right person. But then when I was asked to pitch for it, at that point there’s no other answer but yes.

Kazan: First of all, was it the Austen you liked the most?

Alderton: Yes. It was the one that I’ve always loved because of Lizzie Bennet. I’ve always been obsessed with Lizzie Bennet. She was my hook. But how about you two? Did you ever dream of adapting these texts?

Frost: I was at a place where I said, “I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period.” Netflix asked me to do The Age of Innocence, and it was, I think at that moment, the one book that made me just go, “Oh my God, okay, let me go back and revisit it.” Because I know I love it, but you have to know what the reason is [to adapt it again]. And the thing that totally blew me away on a reread was how relevant and resonant it is. It is about the freedom of the individual versus the conformity of the pack. It has so many themes in it that are really resonant with social media, the bullying of the group.

Alderton [turning to Kazan]: Tackling Cathy, how did you begin? What was your way into that?

Kazan: I think of adaptation as an advanced form of reading. For me, everything I’ve ever written has come from a feeling of “I have to write this specific thing.” When I was 15 and I read the book for the first time, I felt like it literally grabbed me by the throat and wouldn’t let go. And then I just kept coming back to it. And specifically her character, I felt like I had never read anyone like that before or since.

[to Alderton] The BBC’s Pride and Prejudice—is that the one that you—

Alderton: No, that wasn’t my Pride and Prejudice.

Alderton: Yeah, the Joe Wright one was the one that I was more familiar with. But I’m so interested in what you were saying about getting to know Cathy. I was kind of nervous about doing press for a book that’s so beloved, and I’m finding it’s actually been really easy so far because I just know the people so well. So much of it has been basically like, putting Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth, all the Bennet family and Bingley through therapy. That psychological interrogation of these very well-known characters has been the thing I’ve just really, really enjoyed.

Frost: Have you both had to change points of view from the novel? Do you feel like you’ve had to make a specific choice about who you are foregrounding? I think I know the answer in your case, Zoe.

Kazan: No, I actually don’t. I’m aware that the way that I read a book is different from the way that anyone else reads that book. When I read East of Eden, I feel like I see Steinbeck becoming enthralled by this character, finding her as curious as I do. I think he starts out a real place of judgment and over the course of the book, really moves towards love and understanding.

Alderton: I have a similar thing in that for the majority of the book, one of the lead characters is completely unknowable. Not just to Elizabeth, but to the audience as well. So you have to honor that to make it satisfying. That’s kind of frustrating when you’re writing a romantic lead for the first three and a half episodes. None of us, least of all the female protagonist, can see who he is, and we misunderstand him. There is no other option I think than staying with Lizzie.

Frost: It’s very different because the book is entirely from Newland’s point of view. The thing that I wanted to do, and that Netflix were really excited for me to do, was to open it up to find out who the women were.

I think in the book—rightly, because she’s writing from Newland’s point of view—both May and Ellen are sort of constructed as his other. One is the thing to be won, and one is effectively the antagonist. It’s so interesting, because it’s a female author—and [Wharton herself], she’s part Newland. That's who she was growing up. And she’s part Ellen, this woman who now lives in Europe, who's become really cosmopolitan, who is even based on her own love triangle.

The impossibility of that love triangle is the thing I want people to feel. It’s not like one of them is wrong. They're all just feeling what they’re feeling.

Alderton: And how do you feel about bringing that new perspective and analysis to the story? For a book that's so beloved, did you feel excited by that? Or did you feel kind of daunted by it?

Frost: Maybe I should have felt daunted. I didn’t. I think Edith Wharton—it’s so based on her own personal experience of when she was 45, she had this sexual awakening. She was in this really dull marriage. She’d never had an orgasm. When she was 45, she fell in love with this journalist and had this passionate affair.

Frost: She had this big affair, then he ghosted her. But she was trying to make sense of it through this love triangle. When she wrote it, she couldn’t possibly have written herself as a female character in the center of an illicit love triangle because we were still in time of censorship, and she was being published in a very commercial magazine. So she had to make herself the man that has more agency.

Alderton: With any script, you have a relationship with the characters. But with what we are doing, you have this relationship with the writer.

Kazan to Alderton: You’re also a novelist. How are you thinking about bisecting yourself—using both parts of your brain, the novelist part and the dramatist part?

Alderton: I’ll tell you how I felt about it. I’ve written two novels, both of which I’ve tried to adapt. I found it really, really hard. I found adapting Pride and Prejudice incredibly effortless. When I went from Pride and Prejudice to my novel, I was like, "Why is this so much harder? I hate this novelist. Jane Austen is so much easier."

What amazed me is just, it’s like she wrote it to be adapted. It’s like her agent had said to her, “I know you’re going to write this novel about this family of five women, but remember, we could get a great movie deal off the back of it. So try and make it as adaptable as possible.” It has literally been written for TV in this totally perfect six-part structure. I just wish she was around to have written screenplays.

Kazan: This is how I feel about Tolstoy too. When I read War and Peace, I’m like, “Oh, he’s seeing it as if it’s a movie.” It’s very strange to read that so far ahead of the technology to make that possible.

Where was each of your point of entry? What was the first scene that you wrote?

Frost: I always break the whole thing in quite a lot of detail to feel like I understand where the story's going. I think when I actually started writing, I probably wrote from the beginning.

Alderton: I do the same. It’s the only thing that gives me freedom and confidence to write.

Kazan: And did you know how many episodes you wanted from the start, or did that change?

Frost: At one point it was longer, and at one point it was shorter. It’s eight in the end. What about you?

Kazan: I wanted eight originally, and then for budget and logistical reasons, I had to boil it down to seven quite late in the process. I had been four years into adapting it.

Kazan: Yeah. And we were a month away from production, and I had to restructure everything quite late in the game.

Kazan: Yeah, but you know what? It was actually this enormous gift. I had this writing teacher in college, a poetry teacher who talked a lot about constraints. And I don’t know if you've ever seen the... What’s his name? He’s a nightmare, but forgive me—the guy who directed Melancholia.

Kazan: There’s this beautiful Lars Von Trier film called The Five Obstructions, a documentary. He challenges his filmmaking teacher to remake this perfect short film that he made in the 1960s with five sets of obstructions to help him break open his creative process again. And that, combined with what my poetry teacher was always saying—which is the form gives you freedom.

Kazan: I feel like having to... Every time I’ve received, “Okay, we don’t have the money for X, or we don’t have the location for Y, or you have to boil eight episodes down to seven,” that it made me think again about, okay, what’s important here? Seeing the instruction as a gift rather than as an obstacle really just helped me over and over again. I actually gave myself one night to be really mad about it, and then the next day I was—

Kazan: A lot of showrunning, for me at least, has been about learning how to manage my emotions on my own time so that I can go to work and help manage everything. The next day, as soon as I started reworking it, I discovered all of the gifts that it would give me.

Alderton: That lesson is one that you only learn with the privilege of experience. This is only my second TV show. My first, Everything I Know About Love, was an adaptation of my memoir. But I remember now the moments where I said, “If we have to lose this scene, there’s no point shooting the whole show.” Things like that.

Kazan: And then you’re in the edit and you’re like, “Actually, that’s better.”

Alderton: Totally. Or I think back on these things that we couldn’t afford or practically couldn’t work that I really thought would rip out the heart and soul of the show. And now I never dream of an alternate version of that show where those things were put in.

I don’t think I would’ve been as zen as you. I think I would’ve been a petty, grouchy bitch for three days, rather than one.

Kazan: At that point, I was still trying to get my greenlight. I want to hear Dolly’s answer to the first scene question.

Alderton: Oh, sure. So the opening of Pride and Prejudice in the book is obviously setting up the central drama, which is “we need a man. There's a new man in town.” We decided to put Darcy at the very, very top of the show. There is so much in Pride and Prejudice to delight in. What is easy to forget is that it is the best love story of all time. And I’m just like, “We should land that. The first thing we should land is this intrigue between these two characters.”

So Elizabeth is walking around Netherfield Park being kind of nosy and breaking the rules, and she’s intrigued by this man. So much of their attraction to each other, which everyone finds so delicious to read, is that they’re just fascinated with each other, and it takes them a while to work out why. So we wanted to establish that.

Kazan: I love that. I loved her spying and the sort of misunderstanding of who he is.

Dolly, were you wrestling at all about what to do with “it’s truth universally acknowledged,” the most famous line in literature?

Alderton: Andrew Davies gives that line to Elizabeth Bennet, but for me, it felt like it’s the Mrs. Bennet line. The reinterpretation, I suppose, that I’ve done on my Pride and Prejudice is a bit of a justice for Mrs. Bennet. I’m working so hard in this adaptation to really understand why she is the way she is, why she’s so hysterical, why she's seemingly such a social climber. So to give her that line, it felt like we were just off to the races. This is a woman whose preoccupation in life is making sure her daughters are safe. So yeah, it felt like it was an easy line for Olivia [Colman].

When it comes to casting, can you articulate what makes somebody feel appropriate for a period show, versus somebody who seems too contemporary?

Frost: I think for me, casting is really instinctive. Ben Radcliffe, right from his first tape, I was just, “He is Newland Archer. That is the end of the conversation. We are having him.”

Frost: All of them did tapes or auditions. It’s so hard to explain, isn’t it? You see somebody and you just go, “That’s what I have in my head. That’s what we need.”

Alderton: We kind of knew who we wanted Lizzie and Darcy to be, and we had to do chemistry. We did a chemistry [read] with Emma and Jack, and Emma’s an EP on the show. So the minute Jack left, Emma and I looked at each other, and we were like, “That’s totally Darcy.”

But it’s interesting that you were saying that thing about chemistry. I don’t know about you guys, but every time I do casting, I’m amazed how much it feels like falling in love. You go away and you find yourself Googling them and thinking about them and dreaming about them. It’s so wonderful if then they want to do it, and it’s so heartbreaking if they don’t.

Kazan: You fall in love, and then sometimes your love affair doesn’t work out.

Frost: Florence [Pugh] was involved really early, right?

Kazan: She was. I had always had this feeling about East of Eden, and I had sort of tried to ignore that feeling because of my grandfather’s relationship to the material and my relationship to coming from this family. And about a year and a half before this call came, I had written my agent saying, “This is so embarrassing, but if the rights to East of Eden ever come up, can you please let me know so that I can pitch on it?” So they did me a solid. I got an appointment to meet, but I didn’t have a lot of time to prepare.

They asked, “Do you have any actors in mind?” I think I had walked into the room not thinking that I had any actors in mind, and then Florence came out of my mouth. I had seen Midsommar, and I felt like I was witnessing the birth of a genius. And Cathy Ames is such a challenging part that I needed an actor of that caliber. But then we didn’t do any more casting for four years after that.

Kazan: She did. The whole reason this show came together when it did was that there was a window that she had in her schedule. We didn’t have directors yet, and we didn’t have any other cast yet. Her window was starting in October, and between April and June, we put everything together.

So much of it is alchemical. But once you have that central pole that all the spokes are going to come off of, then you start going, “Okay, well if it’s this Lizzie Bennet, it has to be that Mr. Darcy. If it’s this Newland Archer, it has to be this Ellen.”

On the page, East of Eden is the only one of these three novels that has a protagonist who isn’t white. But that isn’t true of your series. I’m curious, Emma and Dolly, if you can speak to that—casting actors who aren’t white in these stories that are largely about white characters.

Frost: Yeah. Edith Wharton came from such a privileged, elite white bubble. That is completely what her life was. But the story is about a man who is chafing against that, and these rules are killing him. So having the contrast of the world inside and outside of that elite white bubble felt crucial to telling this story. And Ellen is part of this really exciting wave of immigration that’s coming into New York at the time, and it’s blowing this old world to pieces. And it’s so much more exciting than this kind of decaying, crusty world that he’s been trapped by.

So for me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters as well that provide that contrast. They are the new ideas, they are the exciting conversations, they are the music that’s coming in. So he was one foot in each, and it was a very organic thing to do.

Alderton: I think there are so many different ways that you can look at diversity with period work. Bridgerton’s a great example of a specific thing. Colorblind casting is a specific example. We decided that we wanted our Pride and Prejudice to be very rooted in historical reality, but we also didn’t want to make an all-white Pride and Prejudice. We wanted to be inclusive and representative. So we just did our homework, and we found cases of families much like the Bingleys who had roots in trade where there were mixed-race families.

Was it the most common thing in Regency England? No. But it’s not the most common thing that a man like Mr. Darcy would’ve married Elizabeth Bennet. It’s so simple in my mind. It’s all made up anyway, and those actors were the best actors for those roles.

Kazan: Can I also say—we have white-presenting actors in East of Eden who have Caribbean roots, and Chinese American people that present as white in our series. I think the idea of whiteness, it can be a weapon. I think it can be weaponized: who we say is white and who we say isn’t white. I just think it’s a funny thing of who we agree is allowed to be in these things and who isn’t.

I do always think it’s a hard thing, because racial identity is such an important part of how people go through the world. And what both of you are saying about finding the logic within your stories for the casting that you want to make, I think, is really important. But I also think it's important to think about how there are identities that are not visible.

Was there one moment from each of your novels that you were the most nervous about getting right?

Frost: I don’t know if it’s one piece of the novel per se, but what gave me pause was trying to find a way into Ellen, Countess Olenska. I wanted to find a way to stay completely true to the spirit and intention of her as a character, but make her emotionally legible to a 21st-century audience. As framed in the novel, there is an element of her being beaten by her husband, and now she needs another man to rescue her. That isn’t this sort of independent, forward-looking woman that I felt I needed at the center of the show.

But Edith Wharton, as ever, is so brilliant that she sort of provided this solution partly through me drawing on her own life, which I used to infuse Ellen. Also, without giving spoilers, there are things that are said about Ellen in the novel that Ellen never confirms. We are in a world of rumor and reputation, and it suddenly became clear to me that what is said about her isn't necessarily true. Once I felt I understood who she was, the whole thing just sort of opened up for me. What about you guys?

Alderton: My take is not so much because of the text—it was because of a previous adaptation.

Kazan: I was going to ask you guys about this.

Alderton: About these adaptations that live in your head.

Kazan: All three of these books have multiple—if not multiple, at least a beloved adaptation.

Alderton: Totally. And on the whole, I feel very comfortable being in this great tradition of every 20 or 30 years, there's a Pride and Prejudice. I like that. I don't want to pretend like there are no other adaptations.

But the one thing that was in my head from the very beginning was the wet-shirt moment. Because it’s such a pivotal moment in the story when we see Darcy for who he is the first time. We understand why he’s been so guarded. We understand why he grips to these social structures so strongly. We understand that he’s a deeply honorable, protective, very recently wounded man.

Alderton: And hot as hell. That’s why the wet shirt was so brilliant, because there’s something about literally seeing the skin of him—literally seeing underneath his carapace for the first time. So I was like, “How are we going to do that?” And I think where I got to in the end is that each generation gets the Darcy that they need, whether it’s Laurence Olivier or Colin Firth or Matthew Macfadyen. The ’90s was a very sexually charged, erotic time in culture, so that’s why we got that Darcy. Matthew, there was something that was kind of cooler about his Darcy.

Alderton: And more indie, which represents his time. And where we are now is a time where masculinity is in crisis. And where Jack instinctively went with his Darcy, it’s quite an honorable place and quite a tender place. So that moment in Pemberley, we actually chose to do it over a series of micro moments that show the softness of Darcy. Which I find very deeply erotic in its own way.

What are your own favorite adaptations, not counting the works we’re speaking about?

Alderton: Mine’s the 1995 Sense and Sensibility. The Emma Thompson Sense and Sensibility.

Kazan: That’s a perfect movie. I love another Ang Lee adaptation, The Ice Storm.

Kazan: Thinking of plays, too—Cabaret is unbelievable, [Liza Minnelli’s] performance and what [Bob Fosse’s] doing with film that he couldn’t do in any other medium.

Alderton: But it still retains the theatricality somewhat.

Kazan: Yeah, completely. I have to shout out to my parents—my parents adapted a lot of films. [Editor’s note: Among other films, her mother, Robin Swicord, wrote Practical Magic and the 1994 Little Women; her father, Nicholas Kazan, wrote Reversal of Fortune.] I just showed my kid their Matilda. When my parents wrote their adaptation, we did a table read when they had their first draft around their dining room table, and I read Matilda.

Kazan: Now my kid is eight, which is about the age that I was then. I got, in that same house, to show her their Matilda. That was really special.

#3456. I Knew Blade Runner 2099 Reviews Would Praise The Visuals, But I’m Surprised By Critics’ Big Critique

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Some Of These Sunrise On The Reaping Reviews Are Brutal, And I Feel Like I Watched A Completely Different Movie

The Cliff Booth Reviews Point Out A Missed Opportunity In Brad Pitt’s Sequel, And I Have To Agree

Enter The World Of Blade Runner 2099 With The Latest Issue Of SFX

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Blade Runner 2099 has arguably been one of the most anticipated titles on the 2026 TV schedule, and there’s a good reason for that. Not only does it expand upon the classic science-fiction franchise, but it also has two capable leads in Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer (who do plenty of stunt work). The show debuts later this week, and reviews are finally starting to roll in. Having seen the show in its entirety for myself, I figured there would be high praise for the visuals, but I am surprised by one particular critique amongst critics.

If there’s anything to know about the Blade Runner universe, it’s that it has major dystopian vibes, and that particular aura is definitely present in 2099. The series continues to highlight a version of Los Angeles in the distant future that’s far from pristine. Surprisingly enough, though, it seems that the show is proving to be a little too dark for some pundits’ liking. Scott Collura of IGN praises the visual style of the series, though he takes issue with just how bleak the proceedings get:

Blade Runner 2099 is a disappointing continuation of the iconic series which leans too heavily into the dark and downbeat side of its future dystopia rather than finding ways to elevate its lead characters in that world. Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are both miscast as a buddy-cop team that subsist on fear and mistrust and angst, while the more interesting characters don’t get nearly enough to do. While the production design, visual effects and overall look of the show are a wonder to behold, 2099 also leans so heavily into its creators’ own fandom at times that it can be distracting.

2099 – which, of course, takes place 50 years after 2017’s Blade Runner 2049 – sees Replicants having become the ruling class, while humans are treated like vermin. At the center of the story is Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human trying to escape her circumstances by posing as a Replicant Blade Runner. In the process of doing that, she is partnered with Olwen (Yeoh), a dying Replicant Runner. The story does indeed get dark, but I didn’t have much of an issue with it. As for The Guardian’s Rhik Samadder, though, he says:

If you’re a cyberpunk who mainlines ennui and likes watching actors you can’t see, speaking words you can’t hear, this show may well knock your fishnet socks off. But why spend this much time immersed in a doomed world, when you could open up a window and watch the real one? It’s live!

Samadder also notably calls the visuals both “impressive” and “oppressive” in a way. However, also mentioning that the series also “plunges us into a far darker world” than the Blade Runner movies (which don’t directly tie into 2099). Likewise, Aaron Pruner of CNET isn’t really a fan of the overly dark setting and aesthetic. In his somewhat mixed review, Pruner praises the show’s execution while also posing this question regarding the bleak vibe:

Could a little bit of levity help break up the monotony? Possibly. But, again, that would go against the grain of the Blade Runner franchise. And not for nothing, the original wasn’t at all funny, yet nuanced characters like Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) and Pris (Daryl Hannah) brought life and color to the dreary, rain-slick streets of Ridley Scott’s original.

The darkness doesn’t seem to be deterring everyone, though, as Alison Herman of Variety has glowing thoughts on the show. Aside from praising Hunter Schafer, Herman also admires series creator Silka Luisa’s adherence to this storied continuity birthed by Philip K. Dick:

‘Blade Runner 2099’ dutifully incorporates the franchise’s visual and thematic touchstones. Despite the passage of time, computer screens still have the blocky, vintage look of early PCs; a psychotically violent replicant named Clotilde (Amy Lennox), an early convert to a cult of personality that promises her and Olwen’s kind eternal life, is a clear echo of Daryl Hannah’s cartwheeling Pris from the original film. ‘Blade Runner’ has always hewn to the beats of a detective noir, and over time, has acquired mainstays of its own that ‘2099’ dutifully nods to.

That’s definitely a big compliment, considering how beloved Ridley Scott’s original 1982 film is and how much critical praise Denis Villeneuve’s 2049 received. Still, not everyone is impressed. TVLine’s Dave Nemetz finds the sci-fi show to be overly bleak as well. Not only that, but he also isn’t too taken with the visuals like a number of others are:

We get it: The L.A. of the future is a rough scene. But there's no spark of joy or hope here to offset the bleakness... just more bleakness. ‘2099’ should at least provide some sci-fi eye candy, but the visuals are a disappointing rehash of the sleek, neon-soaked aesthetic of the original ‘Blade Runner.’

Although I can’t say I saw these critiques about the show’s vibe coming, I can’t blame others for not caring for its dark nature. To me, this kind of style is just baked into the DNA of the franchise, though I can admit that Blade Runner 2099 does delve into murkier territory at times. I’m curious as to how fans will feel when all eight episodes of the show become available for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25.

Erik Swann is a Senior Content Producer at CinemaBlend. He began working with the publication in 2020 when he was hired as Weekend Editor. Today, he continues to write, edit and handle social media responsibilities over the weekend. On weekdays, he also writes TV and movie-related news and helps out with editing and social media as needed. He graduated from the University of Maryland, where he received a degree in Broadcast Journalism. After shifting into multi-platform journalism, he started working as a freelance writer and editor before joining CB. Covers superheroes, sci-fi, comedy, and almost anything else in film and TV. He eats more pizza than the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

#3455. What If We Told You She’s a Mastermind? A Tale of Pop Stardom

A SIDE A child is born in 1989 and grows up on a Christmas tree farm south of Reading, Pennsylvania. She is destined for the stage. She plays Sandy in Grease, Kim in Bye Bye Birdie, Maria in The Sound of Music. A computer repairman teaches her guitar, and she strums untiL her 12-year-old fingers bleed. At 15, she signs with a newly opened record label in Nashville. It’s soon clear that she’s a generational talent. Her name foretells her future fate: the Latin root of celebrity is celere, meaning “rapid,” “fast,” “swift.”

She has romantic associations with celebrities—some of whom treat her ­badly, including a member of a boy band who breaks up with her over a 27-second phone call. By that pOint, she is a celebrity herself. But fame has not warped her the way it has nearly everybody else: She doesn’t even have a manager! What she has are her many great friends. She tells them everything and is pleasantly surprised when they do not put her on blast.

At 29, the record company from Nashville betrays her by selling her life’s work to her archnemesis’s manager. She would have bought the rights to her own songs, only she was never afforded the chance. The sale between the two men occurs without her knowing. When she finds out, she appeals to her loyal fans, who defend her in her moral outrage. With their support, she wins the rights to her music. By then, she’s met her shining knight. After a happy and very public courtship, your English and your gym teachers wed.

When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time, she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.

B SIDE A child is born and grows up on an 11-acre Christmas tree farm that her third-generation banker father bought from a client at Merrill Lynch, where he is a vice president and manages a portfolio around $270 million. When she is 10 years old, the family moves to a 3,560-square-foot, five-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bath Georgian Colonial in Wyomissing, Pennsylvania. A visitor calls the house a “six-star hotel.”

Her mOther is “definitely a theater mom, very aggressive,” says Sandy Carbone, whose son directs The Star in Grease, Bye Bye Birdie, The Sound of Music. The mom asks Carbone’s other son, a computer repairman named Ronnie Cremer, if he might teach her daughter to play a 12-string guitar. “She used to complain a lot about the guitar chords,” Cremer says, “that it hurt her hands.” Cremer relays this to the parents. “Just keep worKing her,” they reply. “She needs this to get better.”

Once, during a lesson, the mother returns home with Taco Bell. The girl, who is not yet a star, scampers to the kitchen, but salad is her lot. “Nobody wants to see a fat pop star,” Cremer recalls the mother saying. (Cremer first told the New York Daily News this story in 2015. The Star declined to comment then. Vanity Fair sent The Star multiple questions while reporting this story; she declined to comment.)

Her father’s connections lead to his daughter singing the national anthem before a minor league baseball game, which leads to another performance, which he videotapes and sends to a marketing manager for the Philadelphia 76ers. Which is how she ends up singing the national anthem for them, wearing red, white, and blue.

Four months into her guitar-playing career, according to Cremer, her father begins driving his daughter to various gigs, giving away tickets to business associates and other acquaintances. Cremer says her father asks that they cheer his daughter loudly so she always seems to be playing to a full house. He captures these performances on tape to send to Nashville, before moving the family there.

Her fame grows. She becomes a Star. Her erstwhile suitors grouse that the songs she writes about them are misrepresentations—that their relationship lasted only a few weeks, or that the call was 27 seconds because she hung up first. In lieu of a manager, what The Star has is her mother and a closed board of stakeholders. Her many friends do not dare speak ill of her—dare not speak of her at all.

By 2006 the father has a stake in the Nashville record company, after making a financial investment worth a reported $500,000, according to Music Business Worldwide. He makes $15 million when it sells. In 2023 she becomes a billionaire on account of her tour, the highest grossing of all time. Her fans do not mind. “Of all the billionaires,” a fan says, “she is my favorite billionaire!”

When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.

A SIDE The Star is beloved. ­Universally, famously. She is friendship bracelets. She is sold-out stadiums. She is honorary degrees. She is a wedding reception for 1,000 and $26 million to charity for the inconvenience to any. She says vote and tens of thousands register. She wears a bandeau “nap top” and midi skirt, and everyone else buys a bandeau nap top and midi skirt. She is our most gracious homecoming queen, our Miss Americana. In these divided times, everybody agrees: The Star is power.

B SIDE Across her 12 eras and interviews with over 100 people who worked with her, who Work with her, who were her confidants, contemporaries, scholars, critics, other anoraks, nemeses, neighbors, classmates, teachers, and lover, what emerges as The Star’s most enduring identity is not musician, not artist, not celebrity, but a combination of victim and victimizer.

The dissenting chorus has penned its own folklore about how The Star often seems to present herself as persecuted even as she sits on a throne of gold and diamonds. Cold, they say, is the steel of her ax to grind. She may not have explicitly ordered her detractors to be banned from parties and other social occasions, or banned her friends from collaborating with her perceived opponents, but tHe results are just that.

Her highness is controlling and manipulative, they say—of charts, of public opinion, of social dynamics. They say she has been known to crucify those who cross her. Others say The Star weaponizes her sense of victimhood, that by foregrounding her own suffering, she believes she is speaking from a position of superior virtue. “She is punitive,” says a music industry professional we’ll call The Exec. “She loves to smack people in the heAd” figuratively, says a person familiar with the matter who used to be close with The Star. We’ll refer to them as The Person Familiar. “This is her way of feeling like she can discipline people.”

A lawyer with knowledge of The Star declined to be interviewed using their own phone, choosing to speak instead through an intermediary. A manager asked for our correspondence to be deleted. A pasTor from her childhood church said they could not speak without express permission from The Star’s family. When these mortals did speak of The Star in public—in line, at the airport, mid-flight, on foot, on the job, at pickup, on the way to grocery stores, parks, or yoga—it was softly, using initials. A Washington Post reporter who recently wrote a book about The Star has noted that countless sources refused to go on the record even to say nice things about her.

Someone who previouslY collaborated with The Star—and asked that their profession not be mentioned because The Star had worked with so few with this specific job—advised I turn down this assignment. Did they think The Star would read the article, though? “Oh yes.”

The Star’s Manichaean notion of the world means “if you’re in the circle, she takes amazing care of you”—according to a musician who toured with her and spoke from behind the scrim of a nondisclosure agreement.

If you’re not, you face social censure. “If you look at history,” says The Person Familiar, “she’s always had villains. Back to her high school days.” Or earlier.

A SIDE When she was young, The Star told Katie Couric in 2009, she had no friends. Or rather, “I had that group of friends when I was about 12. [Then] they all just decided they didn’t wanna hang out with me anymore. I would go and sit dOwn at the lunch table with my friends. And they would get up and move their trays to another table.” If one definition of artist is “a person uniquely sensitive to the vicissitudes of life, from whence their great art comes; someone for whom much happens, and mUch more is expected in return,” then the original pain of The Star appears to be this early sense of loss: the agony of being passed over or feeling lost among peers. No amount of later validation, it seems, would allay it.

B SIDE “That wasn’t true,” says Sharon Luyben. “We had assigned seating in junior high.” (One former classmate of The Star recalls assigned seating at lunch; another isn’t sure. The Wyomissing Area School District did not respond to questions.)

Luyben—Mrs. Luyben to The Star—had been the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High for 34 years. She taught The Star in seventh and eighth grades and then again on Sundays at their church. They first met during a 2002 production of The Sound of Music in which The Star played an older von Trapp child. (She played Maria, the lead, in a different production.)

Chanice Skinner, who sat next to The Star in Luyben’s class, recalls The Star being “always part of the popular crowd,” among preppy kids who wore Ralph Lauren shirts with the collars popped. “If you weren’t part of her friend group,” Skinner says, “you didn’t exist to her.” Years later she was watching a Target commercial in which The Star talked about being bullied. “I was like, You were part of that. What are you talking about? If anything, you were one of the bullies.”

In Skinner’s estimation, The Star’s success, like so many aspects of American life, was overdetermined. “That’s what happens when you have a faMily that is already well-off and able to back you, [to] fund your dream.” Did it seem, though, that The Star carried exceptional promise? “We all had promise,” says Skinner, who starred in plays with The Star and now sells industrial saws in West Reading. “It’s just that she had money.”

Arielle Peppers was a year behind The Star and sat on the other side of Skinner in Luyben’s class for multiple quarters. She remembers The Star coming to class in Ugg boots. Peppers had transferred from the nearby city of ReAding after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck. She asked her mother for a pair of the same boots. “Do you know how much they cost?” her mother said. A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother’s paycheck working variously at a bakery, at a dairy mill, and as a caretaker. Peppers recalls The Star owning multiples of Uggs: “She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one.”

Peppers, who works as a caretaker while maintaining her music practice (under the stage name A.Star), remembers The Star being teased on a single occasion: at a school talent show, when she sang about her crush on a classmate called Corey. (In the aforementioneD 2010 Target commercial, The Star recalls having a crush on a boy named “Corey Robertson” when she was in fourth grade.) The Star had brought her own sound system to perform a song her classmates remember being about “Corey’s eyes.” The Star’s mother helped set it up. The Star won.

The Star’s debut album, released in 2006, includes a song called “Stay Beautiful” that starts like this: “Cory’s eyes”—spelled without the e—“are like a jungle / He smiles, it’s like the radio.”

A SIDE Every Starbucks lover and their mother—or their manager—knows the story. The Star convinces her parents to move to Nashville so she can try her luck in country music. Her music reportedly finds its way to The Machine—an executive from Nashville—in part through his wife, who gets it through a music executive The Star’s father knows. Fame follows.

In time, The Machine decides to sell the label. He tells The Star of his intention and says that he is willing to part with her master recordings—accounting for 50 to 80 percent of the label’s revenue—only if The Star agrees to makE new music in exchange for old, the same bad deal that stymied musicians like Prince and Janet Jackson. The Star has fought many a battle in her time, a great deal of them against men who mean her harm. It is impossible, she cries, to be a woman in the music industry; history proves her right over and over.

A high-profile Manager representing top talent—some of whom have feuded with The Star, including Justin Bieber—hears the news and calls The Machine. On June 28, 2019, The Machine’s board approves a sale, giving The Manager control of The Star’s masters. Two days later The Star takes to Tumblr.

B SIDE Her kingdom terrorized, The Star rises to defend her doMinion. She takes special umbrage with The Manager, accusing him of “incessant, manipulative bullying.” The Person Familiar alleges The Star only ever spoke fondly of The Manager, while The Manager alleges he met The Star only three times, according to The Free Press.

In her Tumblr post, she also mentions an illegal recording of a phone call between her and an archnemesis. The Person Familiar contends they told The Star at the time it was a bad idea to let the nemesis use her name in a certain famous song. Eventually, it seems The Star would come to agree with them.

The Star’s fans send death threats to The Manager. The Manager relays this to The Star’s team; he does not hear from her. He does hear from others who were allegedly smote by The Star for their perceived treachery. They welcome him into the fellowship of the chastened. Mutual friends of both The Star and The ­Manager—a ­singer, a talk show host, an actor—try to help them make up to no avail.

Meanwhile, The Star begins rerecording her old albums, depreciating the value of the originals enough to buy them all back eventually. A hitherto unprecedented feat, it is declared a victory for the people. It’s certainly a victory to The Star, who, in making herself a metonym for all womEn, successfully equates criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.

A SIDE Since her debut in 2006, The Star has been celebrated for her very brilliant songwriting—often about the marriage plot or the pains and possibilities of living in the snakeskin of an ended relationship, but also about historical figures, or literary characters, or herself. There are only so many ways to say “Love me” or “Treat me right,” and she says them all, with tremendous emotional fluency. And she does it all in rhyme, that hooked-up sound so pleasing to the human ear. “There is a reason,” poet Michael Robbins says, “we don’t say penis pic. We say dick pic.”

Also: She is generous to fellow musicians, many of whom open for her, then ascend to new heights of fame. Many remain in her orbit.

Years after opening for The Star on tour, another pop star—let’s call her The Brat—releases her sixth studio album, where she explores the vulnerability she feels next to The Star. Despite the jab, in August 2024, The Star tells New York that she has been blown away by The Brat’s “melodic sensibilities,” calling her lyrics “surreal and inventive.” She adds, “I love to see hard work like that pay off.” In February 2025, The Star is seen dancing jubilantly to The Brat as she performs onstage. The Star is benevolent; she rises above.

B SIDE The Star has historically urged her listeners not to separate the art from the artist, openly turning her life into lyrics and lyrics into hits. It is verboten, however, for others to use her as their source material. Only on her watch may one be casually cruel in the name of being honest.

In 2018, after The Brat opened for The Star, The Star began platonically courting The Brat, inviting her into her inner circle. The Brat shied from The Star’s advances—because...brat—even when she and The Star dated men in the same English rock band.

In 2024, The Brat released a song about her insecurities around the world’s biggest pop star: “I couldn’t even be her if I tried,” she sings. “I’m opposite, I’m on the other side.”

In 2025, The Star seemed to clap back to The Brat by releasing a song of her own about their relationship. In it, she accused The Brat of consuming illegal substances—which is fair enough.

In the time since The Brat released a song about The Star, The Exec says, The Star has “done this performance that she’s supportive of her...but she’s not.” In fact, says The Exec, artists who seem earmarked as The Star’s intentionally DO not collaborate professionally with her rivals, who also seem to be barred from taking part in her social world.

The incident recalled other entangle­ments with other brunettes. A Protégé was affiliated with The Star until 2021, when she sent her debut album to the wife of her archnemesis. Seven-ish weeks later, The Protégé credited The Star on a song, which one occasionally does to ward off litigation and fan outcry, according to copyright lawyers.

In 2023, The Protégé released a song that appeared to intimate a falling-out between her and a once-beloved mentor: “Trust that you betrayed, confusion that still lingers / Took everything I loved and crushed it in between your fingers.” But then, at the 2024 Grammys, The Star was seen vibing to The Protégé’s performance.

Before that was The California Girl—an adult pretending to be a child—and her feud with The Star, who might be a child pretending to be an adult. And, of course, the Kardashian affair, the details of which we are excluding from this narrative. (Yet another protégé, let’s call her The Blonde, remains in The Star’s good graces.)

“It’s truly Regina George,” The Exec says.

There once lived a music critic who dared pan The Star. Around then, members of her friend group, one of whom she lived with, were getting courted by The Star. The Critic felt The Star was “ordering friends from a catalog.” After her negative review ran, The Critic’s friends—professional musicians all, who previously credited The Critic for their early success—shunned her. Her roommate, seemingly of her own accord, asked her to move out of their shared duplex. The Star had won.

A SIDE In a 2020 documentary about herself, The Star repeated a story she has often told about how a big part of her feels frozen at 16, when she became famous. Though if she is frozen at 16, she has repeatedly—and mightily—fought against stasis. In her younger years, she avoided electoral politics, could not see how articulating her opinion was necessary. Later, she found her voice, making statements and endorsements for Democratic candidates, including Kamala Harris for president. She speaks in favor of LGBTQ+ rights, gun control, and making Juneteenth a national holiday. She becomes someone on whom nothing is lost.

B SIDE You only become famous if you really, really want to. Lana Del Rey said as much to the BBC in 2024. And The Star really, really did. “She wants it,” Del Rey said. “She’s told me so many times she wants it more than anyone.”

But if fame is a fickle food, as ­Emily Dickinson—The Star’s sixth cousin, according to Ancestry.com—observed, it is also impunity. You might end up like Barbra Streisand, cloning Coton de Tulears and building a mall in your basement. Or like Jim Carrey, watching YouTube videos all day from your estate in Maui. Or like whatever Elon Musk is doing right now.

Fame also fractures trust. A life grows and shrinks in inverse proportion to the size of its celebrity.

When they were close, The Person Familiar says, The Star’s professional life was run by a cabinet of three, including her mother, who acts as The Star’s manager; her longtime tour manager; and her publicist, to whom we only beg for mercy.

“Nobody is beyond reproach with her,” says The Person Familiar. Perhaps not even The Star’s sometimes close and dear friend who, after their private correspondence spilled across the tabloids as part of a public lawsuit, was not seen at The Star’s wedding. “If you don’t see it her way, she comes after you.”

“It’s always the same,” The Person Familiar says. “They say something she doesn’t like and they are dead to her. She’d be at dinner at [redacted]’s, then three weeks later, ‘Oh no, I hate her guts.’ ”

A/B SIDE Okay, so The Star has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood. Where might she have learned to be so?

Stars function, as cultural theorist Stuart Hall observed, as a mirror. “I want you to know / I’m a mirrorball,” The Star sang in a 2020 hit. “I’ll show you every version of yourself tonight.”

The Star holds up a mirror to us, and what the mirror says is this: If churches were once our society’s primary source of community, identity, and meaning, in these secular times we turn instead to celebrities. And we look, especially, to singers, because who among us is immune to music? The way a song can pitch you forward in space, sustain you through time; the way you swear some songs are written just for you.

A SIDE Stars, they’re just like us. Despite her life in perfect meter, lasting love had long eluded The Star. But it turned out she was a princess, this was a fairy tale, and we were in Hollywood. Her latest beau—regretfully we must call him Redwood—brought to her life a new form of intensity, a golden light, as they courted at a stadium show, a podcast interview, more shows, in Instagram posts. They have so much in common, The Star points out: They both perform at stadiums. He practices; she rehearses. He plays games, she plays shows.

And all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism. Ahead of her wedding, the happy couple donates $26 million to local charities. Since then, The Star released four new songs, launched an Oscar campaign, including performing at the Academy Museum Gala, and got a haircut.

B SIDE Summer 2026. The world’s most famous sexy baby—who insists that she is really a monster on a hill—chooses, as the site of her nuptials, midtown Manhattan during a heat wave. Her guests nibble on buffet food as thousands of New Yorkers lose power.

It is not lost on them that her $26 million giveaway, apart from being a tax write-off, is akin to a person making $81,228—the median household income in New York City—giving away $1,055. (In fall 2025, when this article was commissioned, The Star was worth $1.6 billion. By the time this issue goes to press, she will be worth over $2 billion, or the GDP of Eritrea.)

“To become a billionaire,” The Star’s ex Matt Healy once told the Doomscroll podcast, “you don’t really care that much about culture.” He wasn’t speaking specifically about The Star but the deadening effects of modern wealth. Beyond need lies want. Beyond want, greed.

A/B SIDE And beyond greed was a tricked-out walled garden for the enchanted, her betrothed, and 1,000 of their family and friends, including, according to news reports, at least one government contractor who did not respond to multiple requests for comment. (In March his company took over our nation’s largest ICE detention facility. Earlier this year a father of three was pronounced dead there, after struggling with five guards, the second death at the camp in as many months. His name was Geraldo Lunas Campos.)

In other news, the wedding reportedly featured a raffle where a lucky guest won a Chanel bag. Another allegedly won a 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle. Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. reportedly locked out its own security staff for the occasion, like it was a Mob bar—the kind with no windows. Not even members of the New York Police Department were allowed their own phones on site.

Love may be free, but the performance of it is not. It requires crates, trucks, officers on overtime, private jets, SUVs, HVACs, all the queen’s horses, all the queen’s men, a Jumbotron. Conspiracy theories do not tell you the truth, but they do tell a kind of psychological truth about a place or its people. Had The Star and Redwood filmed the ceremony, perhaps for theatrical release or streaming—maybe on Disney+, which paid The Star a king’s ransom for the rights to another project? (A person with knowledge says the couple has no plans to drop a documentary about their big day.)

Around the barricades of Madison Square Garden, in the wake left by The Star, her groom, and their guests, her fans gathered. Some had been there for hours, wanting to be nearer to their pious majesty. A white truck passed. Pastries—from the merrymaking gentry presumably, though who can say for certain—were distributed, with an assist from a cop in uniform and gear.

If you listened carefully then to the sounds of the city—not for any semantic meaning, but if you were to really pitch your ears to the utopic promise of music—you might have heard the determined whoosh of a weighted blade dropping, dropping, dropping, the ax of public opinion falling in downward demotic motion.

(The Star’s version was used in the making of this article.)

#3454. Goodbye, Mandy: GTA 6 Players Are Already Obsessed With Someone Else

As Grand Theft Auto 6 began releasing around the world last week, players quickly became obsessed with Mandy. She's a neighbor of Jason's who tries to seduce the himbo while he fixes her sink. (And she is totally not a serial killer, no way, why would you ask?) Mandy shows up early in GTA 6. But as more players advance in the game, they're becoming obsessed with a new character: Vicki, a standout character from Chapter 2.

[Ed. note: Light spoilers for the end of Chapter 1 and beginning of Chapter 2 follow. We'll keep them vague.]

After Jason is injured at the end of Chapter 1, Lucia takes him to a run-down motel to lie low. She wants to find stronger painkillers for him, which leads her to Vicki. She's a goth exotic dancer who also moonlights as a small-time drug dealer, and immediately pulls one over on Lucia by selling her over-the-counter Zombix (GTA's brand of painkiller) for $50. Lucia then barges back into Vicki's room and demands the drugs she paid for, which takes the two on a trip around Port Gellhorn. They get Vicki's paycheck from Delights Cabaret and save her friend Dunk from a gang, all the while getting to know one another. They bond over the fact that they're both moms trying to support their kids by whatever means necessary.

Players have quickly fallen for Vicki. "Love her she's my favorite character so far," one player wrote on Reddit.

"Punk Ana de Armas," another said, and, you know, I can kinda see it.

Vicki is voiced by Taryn Manning, who's best known for her role in Orange Is the New Black. She's also starred in 8 Mile, Hustle and Flow, and Hawaii Five-0.

Manning's work as Vicki is part of the reason why players are flocking to her. "Mandy didn't do it for me, but Vicki did because I recognized Taryn Manning’s voice immediately," one Redditor said.

"Vicki the baddie that made everyone move on from Mandy lmao," another said.

Basically, you can tell how far thirsty GTA 6 players are getting in the game based on who they're obsessively posting about over on the Grand Theft Auto subreddits. In a few days, as players continue to marathon Rockstar's hit, I'm sure they'll have a new favorite.

#3453. Jason Sudeikis And Olivia Wilde Had A 'Complicated' Split, But He Does Credit Her For Ted Lasso

Remember when Olivia Wilde was served child custody papers by Jason Sudeikis while she was on stage in front of thousands presenting Don’t Worry Darling at CinemaCon? That was over four years ago in the heat of the pair figuring out the post-split situation. However, these days, the two seem to be on better terms. To that point, Sudeikis is even crediting his ex for the creation of his massively successful TV show, Ted Lasso (which just got big news by the way).

Sudeikis recently said two very notable things about his high-profile breakup. One of those came up when he was on Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso, during which he said his and Wilde's split was “more complicated” and “more human” than how it was portrayed in the media. And on another occasion, Sudeikis went out of his way to talk about how Wilde played a role in getting Ted Lasso made. In his words to the Smartless podcast:

I remember Olivia and I were out to dinner and she's like, 'What are you guys gonna do with that? Like, you guys love doing that thing so much. You should do something with that.' I was like, ‘Yeah.’ And then, her and I just started chatting about it at dinner a little bit like, ‘That would be fun.’

As Sudeikis shared during an interview at a special live edition of the show at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles, Wilde was the person who actually followed up with her then-partner on the Ted Lasso idea years before him and the other creators knew what to do with the character. As Sudeikis continued:

Then Joe and Brendan come out to New York and we hang out for a week in Brooklyn... And then for three days straight, we just start filling up pages of ideas and realize, ‘Oh, this might be a TV show.’ And then we didn't do anything with it for three years.

Wild, right? Mr. Ted Lasso himself, alongside two of his co-creators Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly, sat on the idea for a while until one day they were overflowing with ideas. And then, they sat on it again until this happened. In Sudeikis’ words:

It wasn’t until Bill Lawrence came to me with an idea for another TV show that I was like ‘Ah, this isn’t the right fit.’ He goes, ‘Well, if you have any ideas…’ I go, ‘Well, here’s a stack of papers of stuff we wrote down.’ And he read it, and was like, ‘Oh yeah, there’s definitely a show here.’

Now that Ted Lasso is one of the best shows to watch with an Apple TV subscription, it’s pretty crazy to think how long the whole process took. It took so long that when the idea was first formed Sudeikis and Wilde went from being an engaged couple to splitting up. Thankfully it did, because it’s one of my favorite shows on streaming in recent years.

And did you know there’s even a tribute to Olivia Wilde in Ted Lasso? The AFC Richmond locker room (at one point at least) features Wilde’s actual surname, “Cockburn,” alongside the names of other writers’ friends, family members and former mentors within the production.

Over the past summer, Olivia Wilde spoke a bit to her divorce as well, sharing the conversation that led to their split. Wilde is also having a big year herself, thanks to her latest directorial effort, The Invite, and Sudeikis says he’s “thrilled” for her success. As for him, he just got some good news, as Ted Lasso was just officially renewed for Season 5 by Apple. So the show remains the gift that keeps on giving. In short, thank you, Jason and Olivia!

Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.
